interactions.label: Two patients have identical CBC findings — Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, and microcyti

params.question: Two patients have identical CBC findings — Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, and microcytic hypochromic cells on the smear. Patient A has a ferritin of 68 ng/mL; Patient B has a ferritin of 4 ng/mL. Why is prescribing iron supplements to Patient A harmful?

answers.text: Patient A likely has thalassaemia trait, and supplementing iron causes progressive overload and organ damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Patient A's normal ferritin indicates intact iron stores, pointing to thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency. The body has no efficient excretion pathway for excess iron, so unnecessary supplementation leads to progressive accumulation in the liver and heart.

answers.text: Iron at therapeutic doses triggers haemolysis in patients with adequate iron stores

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Iron supplements do not trigger haemolysis. The danger lies in progressive iron accumulation — without an active excretion mechanism, excess iron deposits in parenchymal organs and causes tissue damage over time.

answers.text: Excess iron is excreted renally, causing iron-induced nephrotoxicity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The body has no efficient renal excretion pathway for iron. Excess iron accumulates in organs like the liver and heart, not the kidneys, which is why iatrogenic overload is so dangerous.

answers.text: Iron supplements suppress erythropoiesis when ferritin exceeds 50 ng/mL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Iron does not suppress erythropoiesis at any ferritin level. The real risk is progressive iron overload in a patient whose microcytosis stems from a haemoglobin synthesis defect, not iron deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Patient A's ferritin of 68 ng/mL means iron stores are intact, pointing to thalassaemia trait. Giving iron to such a patient is harmful because the body cannot excrete excess iron — it accumulates in organs, causing progressive damage.
Well done. Distinguishing thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency before starting treatment is essential — Patient A's normal ferritin is the critical clue that prevents iatrogenic iron overload.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman with menorrhagia has a haemoglobin of 12.5 g/dL, an MCV of 8

params.question: A 30-year-old woman with menorrhagia has a haemoglobin of 12.5 g/dL, an MCV of 86 fL, and a serum ferritin of 8 ng/mL. What is the most accurate interpretation of her iron status?

answers.text: Her iron status is normal because haemoglobin and MCV are within the reference range

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Ferritin drops before haemoglobin or MCV, so waiting for these to fall means missing the earliest and most treatable stage of iron depletion.

answers.text: Her body's iron stores are already exhausted even though haemoglobin production is still adequate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Serum ferritin reflects body iron stores and is the first parameter to fall in iron depletion. A ferritin of 8 ng/mL with normal Hb and MCV indicates storage depletion — the earliest stage, when iron replacement is simplest and most effective.

answers.text: The low ferritin is likely a laboratory artefact since all other parameters are normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A ferritin of 8 ng/mL in a woman with menorrhagia is clinically consistent with depleted iron stores. This is not an artefact — it is the earliest laboratory signal of iron deficiency.

answers.text: She has sideroblastic anaemia with paradoxically low ferritin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In sideroblastic anaemia, ferritin and serum iron are typically elevated, not low, because iron accumulates in mitochondria of erythroblasts and cannot be properly incorporated into haem.

overallFeedback.feedback: Serum ferritin is the first parameter to fall in iron deficiency. A ferritin of 8 ng/mL, even with normal haemoglobin and MCV, means iron stores are already exhausted — this is the optimal window for early treatment.
Exactly right. Ferritin is the earliest marker to fall in iron depletion — recognising this pre-anaemic stage allows intervention before symptomatic anaemia develops.

params.question: A 60-year-old man presents with confirmed iron deficiency anaemia. He is a lifelong vegetarian with no overt blood loss. What should be the first investigation priority?

answers.text: Start oral iron supplements and monitor the haemoglobin response over three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Starting iron without investigating the cause in an elderly man is unsafe. Chronic occult GI blood loss from a colorectal malignancy is the most dangerous cause in this demographic and must be excluded first.

answers.text: Order HbA2 estimation by HPLC to rule out beta-thalassaemia trait

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Thalassaemia trait does not cause iron deficiency — ferritin is normal in thalassaemia. With confirmed iron deficiency in an older male, the priority is excluding GI malignancy, not haemoglobinopathy.

answers.text: Perform upper and lower GI endoscopy to exclude occult malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In older men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anaemia is GI blood loss until proven otherwise. Even without overt bleeding, occult malignancy can cause chronic low-grade blood loss. Endoscopic evaluation is mandatory before attributing the anaemia to dietary insufficiency.

answers.text: Prescribe a high-iron diet with vitamin C supplementation and reassess after six weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While dietary modification may complement treatment, attributing iron deficiency solely to diet in a 60-year-old man is dangerous — it risks delaying the diagnosis of a potentially curable GI malignancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: In an older male with iron deficiency, GI malignancy must be excluded by endoscopy before attributing the anaemia to diet. Chronic blood loss from colorectal malignancy is the most common dangerous cause in this demographic.
Correct. In elderly men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anaemia mandates gastrointestinal evaluation to exclude malignancy — even when a dietary explanation seems plausible.

interactions.label: Anaemia of chronic disease never produces microcytic red blood cells.

params.question: Anaemia of chronic disease never produces microcytic red blood cells.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Anaemia of chronic disease is usually normocytic, but in prolonged, severe cases it can become microcytic. An MCV of 75–78 in a patient with chronic tuberculosis or rheumatoid arthritis suggests advanced, long-standing disease rather than necessarily coexisting iron deficiency.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. While anaemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic (MCV 80–95 fL), it can become microcytic in prolonged, severe inflammation — for example, long-standing rheumatoid arthritis or tuberculosis — as sustained hepcidin activity progressively restricts iron delivery to the marrow.

interactions.label: A patient has microcytic anaemia with an MCV of 62 fL, an RBC count of 6.2 × 10¹

params.question: A patient has microcytic anaemia with an MCV of 62 fL, an RBC count of 6.2 × 10¹²/L (elevated), and a normal RDW. Ferritin and TIBC are both within the normal range. Which condition does this pattern most likely represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In iron deficiency anaemia, the RBC count is typically low (not elevated), RDW is high (reflecting anisocytosis from uneven iron supply), and ferritin is low with a raised TIBC.

Correct. Beta-thalassaemia trait shows a very low MCV with a normal or elevated RBC count, a normal RDW (all cells shrink uniformly — isocytic microcytes), and normal iron studies. This constellation distinguishes it from iron deficiency, where cells vary in size.
Incorrect. In anaemia of chronic disease, MCV is usually normal or only mildly low, ferritin is elevated, and TIBC is suppressed. An elevated RBC count with very low MCV is not characteristic of ACD.
Incorrect. Sideroblastic anaemia shows a dimorphic smear with two cell populations, driving a very high RDW. Ferritin and serum iron are typically elevated, not normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key discriminators are: elevated RBC count (low in IDA), normal RDW (high in IDA, reflecting anisocytosis), and normal iron studies. This pattern — isocytic microcytes with preserved RBC mass — points to beta-thalassaemia trait.

Well done. The triad of very low MCV, elevated RBC count, and normal RDW with normal iron studies is the classic fingerprint of beta-thalassaemia trait — all cells shrink uniformly due to reduced globin chain synthesis.
